headline: Wicopesset Rock on the drop: bonito nosing into the Race, albies flickering early
subhead: Micro-bait has the boulder fields full of finicky speedsters while the stripers stay parked on bunker, waiting on the moon to tighten things up.
body_markdown:
The bait around the boulder fields this week has been small and nervous — silversides and rain bait pushed tight against the rocks off Ram Island and Wicopesset, getting worked over by fish that won't commit to anything bigger than a size 2 fly. That's the tell. When the bait shrinks down like this in early September, it usually means bonito and albies are in residence before the water's ready to give up a real blitz, and that's exactly the read on Fishers Island Sound right now.

We flagged the Race as a zone to watch for bonito last week given the cooler, current-driven water out there, and they've shown up — spotty, but real. The push out of Block Island and Point Judith has reached the western edge of the Sound, with fish working micro-bait hard enough that standard Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters are getting refused more than they're getting bit. Downsizing is the whole game right now. Half-ounce epoxy jigs in bone or pearl, size 1 and 2 Clousers in olive-over-white, small profile Albie Snax in the peanut size — that's what's connecting when the fish show. Best water has been the rip off Wicopesset Rock on the last of the ebb and the seam running off North Dumpling, where the current stacks bait against structure and gives the bonito something to commit to instead of just slashing through and moving on.

False albacore are mixed in but still inconsistent — showing on the same tide stages, same structure, but not holding the way they will once the water cools another few degrees. New London buoy readings have the Sound running around 69°F, with the western end closer to 71°F off Fishers Island. That's still warm enough to keep both species scattered rather than balled up. The pattern to watch is the moon — building toward full on the 6th and 7th, which should tighten the tidal push through the reefs and rock piles and start concentrating bait in a way that makes for a more reliable window instead of a lucky hour here and there.

Striped bass are the frustrating part of the report right now. There's bait around — bunker pods showing off Napatree and drifting into Little Narragansett Bay — but the fish are staged on it rather than actively working it. That's a warm-water problem more than a bass problem. Low-to-mid 70s water keeps stripers lazy and non-committal even with forage stacked up in front of them. The better approach has been eeling the rock piles at Wamphassuc Point and the boulder fields off Ram Island on the front half of the incoming, when the current starts moving fish and bait together instead of leaving them parked in open water. A few bass in the mid-20s to low 30s have come off bucktails worked slow along bottom in 15 to 20 feet, tight to the rocks where the current breaks. Nothing explosive, but a legitimate fish if you're patient with the retrieve and willing to grind through a tide without a bite before it turns on.

Blackfish are starting to show interest again on the Stonington Breakwater and the rock structure around Ram Island as the water eases past its summer high. Green crabs on the bottom in 20 to 30 feet, fished tight to the base of the boulders on slack tide, have been picking at a few tog in the 3 to 4-pound class — early-season fish, not the winter-run bruisers, but a sign the pattern's waking up. This bite will only build from here as the water continues to cool through September.

Fluke are on the same decline everyone up and down the coast is seeing — the back-bay and shallow-flat fish have mostly cleared out of the skinnier parts of Fishers Island Sound, pushing toward deeper structure near the Race and Watch Hill Reef ahead of their fall exit. There are still keeper-class fish to be had on white Gulp and bucktails drifted along the deeper edges, but the numbers are thinning fast and this window is closing. Black sea bass, by contrast, remain a dependable structure bite on the same rock piles — squid strips or Gulp on a light jig around Ram Island and the breakwater rubble continues to produce steady, if unspectacular, action in 20 to 35 feet.

Looking ahead, the next several days should bring more of the same setup — warm enough water to keep the stripers patient rather than aggressive, but a building moon that should start pulling bait tighter against the rocks and reefs. If the bonito push continues at the current pace, expect numbers in the Race and around Wicopesset to build through the weekend, with the first real albie consistency likely following close behind once nighttime temperatures start easing. The stripers are the wild card — once that first genuine cool front comes through and knocks water temps down even a couple degrees, the bunker schools building in Narragansett Bay and along the Sound's western reaches should tighten fast, and that's when the real fall bite through these boulder fields tends to break open. Until then, work the tide changes, downsize the profile, and be ready to move between spots rather than anchoring on one rock and waiting.
